meta.title: Qubit Foundations
meta.subtitle: States, measurement, phase, and single-qubit gates

slides.title: Welcome
body: Quantum computing uses linear algebra because quantum states are vectors and isolated evolution is linear.
Linearity means amplitudes add and can interfere, which is where quantum advantage comes from.
We build intuition with a single qubit and explain why gates must be unitary.
Use the interactive checks and sims to test each idea.

slides.title: Bits vs qubits
body: A classical bit stores one of two values: 0 or 1.
A qubit is a normalized vector in a 2D complex space spanned by $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$.
We write: $$|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle$$
Why this form: any 2D vector can be expressed in this basis with coefficients $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

slides.title: Dirac notation quick read
body: Kets $|\psi\rangle$ are column vectors; bras $\langle\psi|$ are their conjugate transpose.
Basis vectors: $$|0\rangle = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},\; |1\rangle = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}$$
Inner products like $\langle 0|1\rangle = 0$ measure overlap. Orthogonal states do not overlap.
More generally, $\langle a|b\rangle$ is the amplitude of projecting $|b\rangle$ onto $|a\rangle$, and $|\langle a|b\rangle|^2$ is the probability.
The conjugate in the bra ensures phases combine correctly so probabilities are real.

slides.title: Normalization
body: Every measurement must output something, so total probability is 1: $$|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1$$
A state with amplitudes $(\alpha, \beta)$ is valid only if it is normalized.
Quantum gates are built to preserve this normalization.

slides.title: Complex amplitudes
body: Amplitudes can be complex numbers, not just real.
Why complex: phase is needed to model interference, and complex numbers encode phase rotations.
A global phase does not change measurement outcomes: $$e^{i\phi}|\psi\rangle \equiv |\psi\rangle$$

slides.title: Global vs relative phase
body: Relative phase changes the state even if probabilities stay the same.
$$|+\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$$
$$|-\rangle = (|0\rangle - |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$$
These two states measure 50/50, but behave differently under further gates.

slides.title: Measurement
body: Measurement in the computational basis returns 0 or 1.
The probabilities come from squared magnitudes (Born rule): $P(0)=|\alpha|^2$ and $P(1)=|\beta|^2$.
Why collapse: measurement projects onto a basis state, updating the state to match the observed outcome.

slides.title: Bloch sphere intuition
body: Any single qubit can be written as: $$|\psi\rangle = \cos(\theta/2)|0\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2)|1\rangle$$
$\theta$ and $\phi$ locate the state on the Bloch sphere.
Why only two angles: normalization removes one degree of freedom and global phase removes another.

slides.title: State explorer
body: Use $\theta$ and $\phi$ to move on the Bloch sphere.
Notice $P(0)=\cos^2(\theta/2)$ and $P(1)=\sin^2(\theta/2)$.
$\phi$ changes phase, not probabilities, but it affects interference with later gates.

slides.title: Gates are matrices
body: Quantum gates are unitary matrices acting on states.
Why unitary: they preserve inner products, so probabilities stay consistent and evolution is reversible.
Common single-qubit gates: $$X = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$$ $$Z = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$$ $$H = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$$

slides.title: Superposition with H
body: The Hadamard gate creates superposition: $$H|0\rangle = (|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$$
Why: H is a basis change to the $|+\rangle, |-\rangle$ basis.
Now both outcomes are possible with 50% probability.

slides.title: Interference
body: Amplitudes add before you square, which is why interference is possible.
Two Hadamards cancel: $$H(H|0\rangle)=|0\rangle$$
Why: the paths add with opposite phases, so the $|1\rangle$ amplitude cancels.

check.prompt: Check: What is the gate identity $$H Z H = ?$$
check.hint: It turns phase into a bit flip.
check.explain: Correct - H Z H equals X.

slides.title: Phase vs bit
body: The Z gate flips the phase of $|1\rangle$: $$Z|1\rangle = -|1\rangle$$
A phase flip can become a bit flip after a Hadamard: $$HZH = X$$
Why: H swaps the phase and computational bases, converting phase into amplitude.

slides.title: Rotations
body: Rotation gates move you smoothly on the Bloch sphere.
A common example is the Y rotation: $$R_y(\theta)=\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{bmatrix}$$
Why rotations matter: any single-qubit unitary can be built from rotations.

slides.title: Expectation values
body: Repeated measurements estimate probabilities.
Example expectation value of Z: $$\langle Z \rangle = |\alpha|^2 - |\beta|^2$$
This tells you how biased the state is toward $|0\rangle$.
Why use it: expectation values summarize many shots into a single observable.

slides.title: Interactive qubit lab
body: Apply gates, watch the state update, then measure.
Try: H $\to$ Z $\to$ H (a phase flip becomes a bit flip).
Try: H $\to$ Measure multiple times to see 50/50 outcomes.
Use $R_y$ to rotate by a custom angle and watch probabilities change.

slides.title: Next steps
body: Two-qubit systems introduce entanglement: $$|\Phi^+\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$$
Why it matters: entangled states cannot be factored into separate qubits.
See the next lessons for circuits and multi-qubit ideas.
